strengths: Resolves an open problem from COLT 2025 on the parameterized complexity of ReLU network verification and zonotope containment, providing W[1]-hardness and ETH-based lower bounds for a broad set of fundamental problems.

The core reduction from Multicolored Clique to 2-layer ReLU positivity is technically novel and elegant, using Sidon sets and carefully designed spike/penalty gadgets so that the input dimension grows linearly with the clique size.

Establishes matching ETH lower bounds showing that simple enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal in the exponent of the input dimension, giving a tight complexity picture for positivity, surjectivity, zonotope containment, and Lipschitz-constant computation.

Extends hardness to zonotope non-containment via the known duality with 2-layer ReLU networks, and to Lp-Lipschitz constants for both 2-layer and 3-layer networks, thereby settling multiple open questions simultaneously.
Includes positive tractability results for input convex neural networks and a randomized FPT approximation based on subspace embeddings, adding useful balance to the negative results.
weaknesses: The paper is purely worst-case theoretical and contains no empirical evaluation or algorithmic experiments; while appropriate for a complexity paper, it limits direct evidence of practical impact.

The practical relevance is somewhat constrained by the highly structured gadget constructions; the paper acknowledges this but does not fully characterize which realistic low-dimensional manifold assumptions might avoid the hardness.
The positive algorithmic results are relatively minor, and the randomized approximation has worse worst-case running time than existing sampling-based methods, as the authors themselves note.

There are minor presentation inconsistencies, e.g., L0-Lipschitz constant appears in Corollary 6.1 while the conclusion lists it as open for 2-layer networks, and the XP definition contains a small typo.
Several key proofs are only sketched in the main text; although the appendix contains details, the main narrative could better highlight the proof ideas for the Lipschitz and zonotope results.

strengths: Resolves the open problem of the parameterized complexity of 2-layer ReLU positivity, surjectivity, and zonotope non-containment with respect to input dimension d, a significant advance in neural network verification theory.
Provides strong ETH-based running time lower bounds (ρ(d)·N^{o(d)}) that show brute-force enumeration is essentially optimal up to constant factors in the exponent.
Introduces a novel reduction from Multicolored Clique using Sidon-set labels, spike/penalty functions, and homogenization to eliminate biases, which is technically sound and carefully constructed.
Extends hardness results to Lp-Lipschitz constants for all p∈(0,∞] and to 3-layer approximation, covering a broad range of verification-related problems.
Includes positive results for input convex neural networks (L1 poly, L∞ FPT) and a randomized FPT approximation via subspace embeddings, adding breadth.
The theoretical claims are well-supported by detailed proofs in the appendix, with appropriate comparisons to prior work.
weaknesses: The main text frequently defers to proof sketches; while the appendix contains full proofs, the main narrative could be more self-contained for a top-tier venue.
The randomized approximation algorithm in Section 7 has worse worst-case running time than existing methods, and its practical advantage is largely speculative.
The parameterized complexity of Lp-maximization on zonotopes for p∈(1,∞) remains open, so the classification is not fully complete.
Minor presentation issues: the proof of Proposition 6.3 could more explicitly connect dual norms to L1/L∞ constants, and the extracted text shows occasional typos.
Implications for practical neural network verification are discussed only briefly, which may limit the paper's impact on applied subareas.

strengths: Resolves a prominent open problem from COLT '25 on the parameterized complexity of ReLU network verification and zonotope containment, proving W[1]-hardness and matching ETH lower bounds.

Provides strong ETH-based running-time lower bounds showing that naive enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal for multiple fundamental problems, including positivity, surjectivity, approximating the maximum, and Lp-Lipschitz constants.

The reduction from Multicolored Clique to ReLU positivity is nontrivial: it carefully constructs spike and penalty functions using Sidon sets so that the input dimension grows only linearly with the clique size.
Extends known NP-hardness results to W[1]-hardness for all p in (0,∞] for 2-layer Lp-Lipschitz constants and for approximating Lp-Lipschitz constants in 3-layer networks.

Includes positive tractability results for input convex neural networks (ICNNs) and a randomized FPT-approximation for norm maximization on zonotopes via subspace embeddings, adding balance to the hardness results.
The paper is well organized, with clear proof sketches in the main text and detailed proofs in the appendix, making the technical arguments reproducible for experts.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical and includes no empirical evaluation, although this is appropriate for a computational complexity contribution.

Several results are extensions of known NP-hardness to the parameterized setting (e.g., Lp-Lipschitz constants, zero-function check), so the incremental novelty for those specific problems is moderate compared to the core positivity/zonotope result.
The proof for p in (0,1) in the appendix is restricted to rational p, while the theorem statement claims all p in (0,∞]; there is a potential gap for irrational p that is not addressed.
The positive results for ICNN L1/L∞ Lipschitz constants rely on an external extended formulation from Hertrich and Loho (2024), so the paper's contribution there is somewhat dependent on prior work.

The parameterized complexity of several problems is not completely settled (e.g., W[1]-membership for 2-layer ReLU positivity, exact complexity for Lp-maximization on zonotopes for p in (1,∞)), though the paper acknowledges these as open questions.

strengths: Resolves a major open problem of Froese et al. by proving W[1]-hardness of 2-layer ReLU positivity and zonotope non-containment with respect to the ambient/input dimension.

Establishes a broad and coherent set of parameterized hardness results: W[ℓ-1]-hardness for positivity/surjectivity, W[ℓ]-hardness for deeper Lipschitz approximation, and matching ETH-based lower bounds showing brute-force enumeration is essentially optimal.

Introduces interesting technical machinery, including a Sidon-set-based reduction from Multicolored Clique, homogenization to remove biases, and connections between bounded-depth ReLU networks and the W-hierarchy.
Extends results to several related problems, including network verification, zonotope containment, Lp-Lipschitz constants, injectivity, and convexity/representation by 2-layer networks.
Provides upper bounds, including XP algorithms and W[P] containment for several cases, plus some positive tractability results for input-convex networks and a randomized FPT approximation.
The paper addresses core problems in neural network verification and computational geometry with clear relevance to AI theory and verification.
weaknesses: The paper is very dense and notation-heavy; several proofs, especially in Sections 5 and 7, are difficult to follow, with parameter choices (e.g., ε and U) and case analyses that would benefit from more explanation.

The auxiliary zonotope-sparsification result in Theorem 8.1 appears to have a technical issue: the construction A' = (2b_i' + c) does not obviously preserve the claimed containment, since adding c to every generator changes the center of the zonotope. This is peripheral but weakens the positive-result section.
Some hardness claims depend on concurrent or recent works for Lp-norm maximization on zonotopes, limiting independent novelty for those particular statements.
There is no empirical evaluation, which is acceptable for a theory paper but would benefit from a brief discussion of practical implications for neural network verification and robustness.

A few statements in the abstract and table are slightly imprecise, e.g., the phrasing linking positivity and surjectivity across layer counts, and the parameter-ℓ results are sometimes stated informally.

strengths: Resolves multiple open problems regarding the parameterized complexity of ReLU network verification and zonotope containment, including the open problem posed by Froese et al. at COLT 2025.

Provides a comprehensive set of W-hardness results for positivity, surjectivity, Lipschitz constant computation, and zonotope non-containment, establishing near-optimality of brute-force enumeration under the ETH.

Introduces novel and technically sophisticated reductions from Multicolored Clique and Weighted (Anti)Monotone t-Normalized SAT to ReLU networks, carefully handling bias removal and parameterization by input dimension and depth.
Includes positive tractability results for input convex neural networks and a randomized FPT-approximation algorithm using subspace embeddings, adding balance to the hardness results.

The paper is well-structured, with rigorous proofs and clear connections to the W-hierarchy, potentially inspiring further research at the intersection of parameterized complexity and neural network verification.
weaknesses: The paper is extremely long and dense, which may make it difficult to review and potentially exceeds typical conference page limits; a more concise presentation would improve readability.

The work is purely theoretical and lacks empirical validation or practical algorithm implementations; while appropriate for a theory paper, this may limit its immediate impact on practitioners in the AI community.
Some proofs contain minor typographical or phrasing errors (e.g., in Theorem 7.3, the condition 'V_i(x) ≤ T' appears to be a typo for 'V_i(x) = 0'), which could momentarily confuse readers.
The main contributions are largely negative hardness results; although the paper includes some positive results, the overall tone may be seen as less constructive for an AI audience.

strengths: Resolves several open problems on the parameterized complexity of ReLU network verification, zonotope containment, Lipschitz constants, and injectivity, including questions posed at COLT '25.

Provides a comprehensive set of W-hierarchy hardness results parameterized by input dimension and by depth, with matching ETH-based running-time lower bounds showing that naive enumeration is essentially optimal.
Establishes interesting and useful connections between neural network verification, zonotope containment, norm maximization over zonotopes, and parameterized complexity theory.
Includes both hardness and upper-bound results, such as XP algorithms, W[P]-containment for several cases, and tractability/FPT approximation for restricted classes like input convex networks.
The technical constructions, especially the reduction from Multicolored Clique to 2-layer ReLU positivity and the homogenization technique, appear original and powerful.
Well-positioned relative to recent literature, with clear discussion of implications for practice and open questions.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical, with no empirical evaluation; its impact may be concentrated in the complexity/theory community rather than broadly across AI.

Some proofs are very dense, and the provided manuscript has formatting/extraction issues that make a few technical arguments hard to verify in detail (e.g., the reduction proof in Theorem 7.3 appears partially garbled).
There are minor typographical and presentation issues, such as 'welt' instead of 'weft', awkward table formatting, and a likely typo in Theorem 5.10's running-time statement.
Several concurrent independent works are cited; although the paper positions itself relative to them, the exact incremental novelty versus these concurrent results could be clarified further.
